title: The Appendix Is in the Past Tense
deck: The appendix may place Oceania within a retrospective view. But its grammar offers a formal clue, not proof that the regime has fallen.
body: Edition note: Complete English translation of the Chinese essay. Full-book spoilers.
The novel's last sentence is: he loved Big Brother.
Turn the page, and there is something else.
Its title is “The Principles of Newspeak.”
Most readers skip it.

It looks like a technical explanation: the grammatical rules of Newspeak, the three categories of vocabulary, how certain words are simplified, why “free” can only be used in sentences such as “this dog is free from lice.”
It reads like a guide to the fictional world, attached to the end of the novel.
And it has one particular feature.
It is written in the past tense.
The tense of those sentences
Look at the way the appendix begins.
Its approximate meaning is: Newspeak was the official language of Oceania, designed to meet the ideological needs of Ingsoc.
“Was.”
The same register continues throughout. It describes what Newspeak was intended to do, how its vocabulary was classified, what the A, B, and C vocabularies were each used for.
It also says something more important: Newspeak was expected to replace Oldspeak entirely around 2050.
“Was expected.”

The past tense places the appendix in a narrative position looking back at 1984. “Was expected” records a plan; by itself, it does not prove that 2050 has already passed or that the plan failed. It is an important formal clue, not proof of a historical outcome.
There is something more direct, too.

Discussing the translation of classic texts, the appendix notes that translating works from Oldspeak into Newspeak was extraordinarily difficult and proceeded slowly. Its examples include a passage from the Declaration of Independence.
And this appendix is written in Oldspeak.
Not Newspeak. Standard, complex English, with subordinate clauses, capable of expressing abstract concepts.
What does this mean?
Now put these things together.
First, the appendix is written in Oldspeak.
Second, it discusses Newspeak in the past tense.
Third, it presents 2050 as an expectation held at the time, without telling us whether that expectation was later fulfilled.
Fourth, it can clearly explain the intention behind Newspeak's design, including which thoughts it was meant to eliminate.

As the first essay explained, the whole point of Newspeak is to make certain thoughts impossible to assemble. If Newspeak succeeded, no one could think “this language is designed to restrict thought,” because the words needed to assemble that thought are precisely the ones that have been deleted.
Yet the appendix explains this with perfect clarity.
We can therefore read its voice as looking back from a time after Ingsoc.

It can write in Oldspeak and analyze how Newspeak restricts thought. But the novel does not specify the date from which this voice speaks. Grammar alone cannot make “Oceania has fallen” an explicitly stated historical fact.
What Orwell did
This is not the only possible grammatical explanation, but it is a reading grounded in the text.
The American Book-of-the-Month Club once asked for the appendix to be removed. Orwell refused.
In this reading, its position after the main narrative is crucial.
There is a reason for that position.
Placed at the front, it would be a manual. Readers would carry its explanations into the narrative, and it would simply help them understand the setting.
Placed at the end, it at least creates a measure of narrative distance.
The reader has just finished watching Winston being utterly destroyed, just read “he loved Big Brother,” just accepted that the defeat is complete and irreversible.
Then the page turns, and a voice speaks about all this in the past tense.
That voice does not say “they were overthrown afterward.” It depicts no uprising, no victory, no consoling scene of any kind.
It simply shifts into a retrospective register. This offers a clue for the reading that Oceania is not eternal, without putting a seal of certainty on it.
This is not hope
We must be clear about this, or the essay will slide into a cheap reversal.
The appendix does not tell us what later happened to Oceania.
If it really does speak from after Ingsoc, whether the regime was overthrown, collapsed from within, lost a war, or gradually became something else over a long period: the appendix says not a word.
Nor does it say that Winston is saved.

The novel does not explicitly say whether Winston has already been executed by the ending. But his former judgment and love have been destroyed from within. In the end he sincerely loves Big Brother; there is no room for doubt about that. Julia, too, admits that she has betrayed him. The scene in the park, where the two have nothing to say to each other, is real.
The appendix can offer them no compensation.
It does not make those things not have happened.
So it is not hope.
It says something else, something much colder and harder:
if we accept the reading that the appendix comes from after Ingsoc, then the attempt was never completed.
What was the attempt trying to complete?
Return to the formulation in the first essay.
What this machinery seeks is not rule, oppression, or exploitation. History is full of those.
It seeks to cover a person completely, leaving no gap at all.
Newspeak closes gaps in language. Doublethink closes gaps in feeling. Altering the records closes gaps in fact. Room 101 closes the last gap, that “in my heart I still love her.”
With Winston, it succeeds.
O'Brien has said that they will not allow a single mistaken thought to exist anywhere in the world, however deeply hidden and however harmless.
Notice the words “in the world.”
Not “within our Party,” not “in this country.” In the world. Not a single one left.
That is the scale of the attempt: it wants not most, but all.
And the more cautious judgment the appendix can support is that at the very least, “all” may not have been achieved.
Because if it had been, no one could afterward explain the design of Newspeak so clearly in Oldspeak. The position from which it could be explained was itself supposed to have been deleted.
That position remains.
The demand to leave “not a single one”
We can now state the series' final judgment.
A system seeking to cover people completely must continually eliminate the remainders it cannot control. The appendix keeps open the question of whether it can do so forever.
Not because it is insufficiently ruthless. It has already taken ruthlessness to the limit, as far as dismantling a person's arithmetic.
Not because someone resists. Winston resists. Julia resists. Both are crushed flat. Resistance does not work.
But because the demand for “all” cannot itself be fulfilled.
The second essay discussed this: the Party can raid the room and take the lovers away. It cannot make those months not have happened.
The coffee has been drunk. The afternoon has passed. Those things happened.
And what has already happened is the one thing the machinery cannot deal with.
It can burn the photographs, alter the newspapers, make everyone say it never happened, make even the last person who remembers forget.
It cannot make the thing not have happened.

The glass paperweight is smashed, and the tiny piece of coral rolls across the floor. But someone once held it in his hand and found it beautiful. There is no record of that, no witness; afterward, even Winston no longer remembers it.
It still happened.
The woman doing the washing
There is someone in the book who appears many times and never has a name.

She is a woman living in the courtyard behind the junk shop, a prole, very stout, with rough hands. Every day she hangs out washing in the yard and sings as she works. The song is machine-made popular music for the proles: trite words, a simple tune.
And she sings it beautifully.

Winston watches her through the window. He has thought about this: the proles make up eighty-five percent of the population, yet the Party does not train and constrain them as it does its members. But the Thought Police still monitor them and remove anyone who might pose a threat.
They do not have to undergo the rigorous ideological training imposed on Party members. Their days revolve more around having children, working, drinking, gambling, quarreling, and singing.
That elaborate machinery has not covered their lives to the same depth.
Winston has written in his diary: if there is hope, it lies with the proles.

And the book also shows the problem with this thought: they are not all illiterate, but they lack organization and have not turned their strength into collective political action. In the novel, this road leads nowhere.
Both statements are true.

But this series is not saying “hope lies with the proles.” It is saying that the machinery intended to cover everything has reached into that courtyard, but has not exhausted the meaning of that woman's singing.
The woman hangs out her washing and sings a bad song made by the Party, and she sings it beautifully.
This appears in no plan.
A final word
We can now look at the four essays together.

This is no ordinary tyranny. Its goal is far more specific and far larger: to cover a person completely. Newspeak makes certain thoughts impossible to assemble; doublethink keeps contradictions from causing friction; rewriting the records leaves no original for comparison; and Room 101 takes away the last “in my heart I still.”

Two people live in those gaps for a few months. What they want is absurdly small: real coffee, lipstick, a glass paperweight, an afternoon lying down and looking out of the window. These things are of no use at all in overthrowing the regime, and it is precisely because they are of no use that they belong to them. The room is a trap prepared for them. The taste of the coffee is not.
Then they are arrested, taken apart, and remade. In the end, Winston sincerely loves Big Brother. This is complete defeat. There is no getting around it.
And the book is not over.

Turn the final page, and there is an appendix written in Oldspeak. It discusses Newspeak in the past tense and presents 2050 as an expectation held at the time, not as an outcome whose success or failure the narrative has confirmed.
It gives us grounds to imagine a voice speaking from after Ingsoc, without turning that possibility into an explicit ending.
It does not tell us how things ended. It depicts no victory. It cannot make Winston's life any easier to bear.
It simply speaks from a position that was supposed no longer to exist.
The machinery wanted not a single one left.
And the appendix at least prevents us from being certain that it succeeded.
The regime demands eternity. The novel does not award it eternity.

George Orwell, Nineteen Eighty-Four, published in 1949. Names and terms in the Chinese essay follow Dong Leshan's translation. The appendix discussed here is “The Principles of Newspeak,” which follows the main narrative.

review.full_reread: Read all four Chinese bodies and all four complete en translations, titles, decks and index. Reread every changed unit against the final approved wording and its surrounding argument. Earlier review evidence is retained in review_history, not current pending status.
review.structure: All paragraph, heading and inline-emphasis boundaries preserved; all unamended prose units unchanged.
review.interpretive_boundaries: Original authorial judgments retained. Source observations outside the approved change set remain historical context; this pass makes no new claim of exhaustive independent novel or publication-history verification.
semantic_checks: Photograph: conscious recognition and concealment, then destruction after about ten minutes through fear; no reflex or pre-awareness claim remains.
Private life: the Brotherhood attempt remains explicit, while value exceeds usefulness to resistance; deliberate suppression of sexual pleasure is not confused with a forgotten prohibition.
Dress is a future intention while Julia remains in overalls; lipstick replaces the invented worn dress in both sensory examples.
Julia rejects the earlier dead claim and repeats it only just before arrest; present life is distinguished from distant political victory.
Cross-references now point to essay three; forbidden book arrives later through a briefcase exchange.
Pain is controlled by a dial, without asserting an electrical mechanism; the two final sentences are the ending of the main narrative.
Publication: American Book-of-the-Month Club deletion request and refusal; the importance of final placement is explicitly the essay’s reading.

Proles: less intensive ideological training coexists with surveillance and removal of threats; no blanket illiteracy claim; the courtyard is reached by power without exhausting the meaning of the song.

Preserved the complete room/trap/real-experience argument, authorial claim that past events cannot be undone, stronger judgment about totality, and cautious appendix reading without supplying a new proof or ending.

review_history.stage: Complete-translation review before approved source corrections

review.coverage: All 106 source units translated in order, including eight headings, every qualification about the appendix, the historical-irreversibility argument, the washing woman, and the four-essay synthesis.
prior_edition_findings: The previous approximately 491-word rewriting focused almost entirely on the appendix as a formal refusal of eternity. It omitted the publishing anecdote, the demand to leave no remainder, the past event that cannot be undone, the washing woman and proles, and the full four-essay synthesis.

Its newly framed “more defensible hope” displaced the source's emphatic “this is not hope” and its separate argument about what has already happened. The complete translation restores those distinctions.

source_questions.issue: The refusal to cut the appendix is documented. The proposed move to the front, and a refusal specifically on placement, were not verified. Retained pending author decision.

Absolute claims that the Party did not govern the proles, and the blanket illiteracy claim, are too broad. Part I, Chapter 7 describes Thought Police among the proles and the elimination of potential threats, while distinguishing this from systematic Party indoctrination. Retained pending author decision.

The source moves from a cautious reading of the appendix to an authorial argument about the impossibility of undoing events. This is a substantive interpretive judgment, not a translation error. It is preserved without supplying a new proof or weakening it.

review.style: Preserves the conditional reading of the appendix, the distinction between interpretation and stated historical outcome, and the author's separate stronger judgment. No rescue of Winston or invented history after Ingsoc is added.
review.full_reread: All source and translated units were reread together as the four-essay batch; structure, emphasis, voice, transitions, and unresolved source claims were checked.
